title: Teaching

Instructor – University of Washington


Course: ECON 200 Introduction to Microeconomics

Selected Student Comments:  “This was my first econ class, but I thought the topics were incredibly interesting. I found myself applying so many of the concepts that we learned to other thinks in my daily life. Overall it really made me think and I enjoyed it.” “What contributed most to my learning was asking clarification questions to the Professor because they really helped me clear my doubts.”  “I appreciated how Frida was wiling to re-explain a concept that someone didn’t get and really took the time to make sure our questions were getting answered. Examples she drew on the chalkboard during class time were very thorough and useful.”

title: About Me
text:
I am a Ph.D. Candidate in Economics at the University of Washington.
My research focuses on macroeconomics, public finance, and household behavior, with an emphasis on how bargaining power, family dynamics, and taxation shape female labor supply across the life cycle.
I use structural life-cycle models, rich panel data, and policy simulations to understand how households make decisions under uncertainty and under institutional constraints.
I am committed to undergraduate teaching and inclusive pedagogy.
Outside of research, I enjoy creative writing, tennis, bird-watching, and exploring the Pacific Northwest.

title: Research
text:
(Job Market Paper)
PDF
I examine how intra-household bargaining, endogenous divorce, and gender-education-specific marital preferences shape female labor supply across the life cycle.
Using a structural model calibrated to Japanese survey data, I show how bargaining power, education, assets, and divorce expectations jointly drive female participation patterns, consumption, and savings.
The extended model on intensive working hours decision quantifies the distortions created by progressive household taxation and evaluates alternative tax reforms.
Presentations: American Economic Association 2026 (scheduled, poster), Gender in the Economy: Structural Transformation and Women’s Time-Use 2026 (submitted)

title: Research
section: Financial Literacy Confidence and Retirement Planning: Evidence from China (Research Assistant for Bingzheng Chen and Ze Chen)
text:
Financial Literacy Confidence and Retirement Planning: Evidence from China (Research Assistant for Bingzheng Chen and Ze Chen)
PDF
In this paper, we conduct a survey to examine how individual’s financial literacy confidence bias affects their retirement planning behaviors in China. The survey measures both the respondent’s subjective and objective financial literacy, as well as their assessment and actual actions with respect to their retirement planning. We find that financial literacy overconfidence significantly promotes individual’s retirement planning behaviors. Our results contribute to understanding the effect of subjective financial literacy on retirement planning.
Published: Risks (February 2023)

title: Research
section: Increasing Return to Experience, Social Norm, and Female Labor Supply
text:
Increasing Return to Experience, Social Norm, and Female Labor Supply
I extend my structural framework of Job Market Paper to incorporate human capital accumulation and increasing returns to experience. Combined with social norms on wife’s share of child care, the structural life-cycle model will be able to rediscover motherhood penalty under a new light.
